drivers.name: Price increase (2.3%)
drivers.evidence: Two prior weeks at $6.56: 24 and 53 units (vs baseline 44.8), noise-adjusted effect x0.87

drivers.evidence: Planner note indicates supply risk, likely reducing consumer demand due to stockout fear

adjustment.analysis: Baseline median is 44.8. No events in target week. Price increased 2.3% to $6.56, a level seen in 2026-09-28 and 2026-10-05, which sold 24 and 53 units (vs baseline 44.8), giving a noise-adjusted effect of x0.87. The supplier delivery warning adds supply risk, lowering demand confidence. No past promotion at this price. The classical uplift model suggests x1.0, but price increase and supply risk justify downward adjustment. Evidence is moderate (2 data points at same price, one supply note). Shrink toward 1.0 for thin evidence.

brief:
PRODUCT: Ice Cream 1.5L | category Frozen | Store #12 (Austin, TX)
TARGET WEEK: 2026-10-19 to 2026-10-25 (2 weeks after the last week with sales data)

KNOWN PLAN FOR THE TARGET WEEK:
  events: none
  shelf price: 6.56 (+2.3% vs regular price 6.41)
  planner notes: Supplier warns of a short delivery

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 44.8 | 5%-95%: 18.6 - 69.4 | 10%-90%: 25.6 - 65.9

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-36% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
